Furthermore, degenerative changes occurred in all groups, but intra-articular injection of SPIO-ASCs or ASCs alleviated these degenerative changes. Prussian blue staining indicated that the implanted ASCs were directly associated with the regenerated tissue. Overall, targeted intra-articular delivery of SPIO-ASCs promoted meniscal regeneration whilst providing protective effects from osteoarthritic damage.

title: The new era of anticoagulation
Application of Tranexamic Acid in Trauma and Orthopedic Surgery
abstract: Tranexamic acid has gained recent interest in orthopedics and trauma surgery because of its demonstrated benefit in several clinical trials. It is inexpensive and effective at reducing blood loss and blood transfusion requirements without a significant increase in morbidity or mortality. The optimal timing, dosing, and route of administration in orthopedics are yet to be elucidated. Significant investigation of tranexamic acid use in joint replacement and spine surgery has promoted its incorporation into the everyday practice of many of these surgeons. The paucity of studies regarding its use in orthopedic trauma has limited its integration into a field that may stand to benefit most from the drug.

title: Tranexamic acid in anesthetic management of surgical procedures
abstract: Blood loss during surgical procedures poses a grave risk to the patient, but transfusion is costly and associated with adverse outcomes. Antifibrinolytics, however, offer an economical and effective means of decreasing blood loss associated with surgical procedures. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is an antifibrinolytic that blocks lysine-binding sites of fibrinogen and fibrin, preventing the breakdown of existing clots. This journal course reviews extensive research demonstrating that antifibrinolytics such as TXA decrease blood loss and in some studies reduce allogeneic transfusion requirements. In addition, this journal course addresses concerns that use of antifibrinolytics increases embolic events, reviews research that demonstrates TXA does not increase the incidence of vascular occlusive events, and describes methods of TXA use in cardiac and orthopedic surgical procedures, neurosurgery, and obstetrics. The Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetist should consider the possibility, on a case-by-case basis, of using TXA in surgical procedures to reduce blood loss with minimal adverse effects.

title: The effect of leukocyte depletion in PRP on the proliferation and chondrogenesis of synovium-derived MSCs and expanded chondrocytes
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is nowadays widely applied in different clinical scenarios, such as orthopedics, ophthalmology and healing therapies, as a growth factor pool for improving tissue regeneration. PRP has been advocated as one of treatment strategies for cartilage tissue regeneration. To date, several different platelet-rich formulations have been available, but a deep knowledge of their composition and mechanism of action in a specific clinical use is needed. The effect of PRP on chondrocytes has been studied using in vitro and in vivo basic science models. A recent systematic review of this literature demonstrated that 71% of the studies report PRP increases the synthetic capacity of chondrocytes, including up-regulation of gene expression, proteoglycan production, and type II collagen deposition. However, only 4.8% (1/21) of reports included in this analysis characterized the leukocyte, platelet, and red blood cell (RBC) contents of their PRP formulations. There are many variations in PRP formulations, with both platelet and leukocyte concentrations having been identified as major constituents affecting the inflammatory responses after PRP injection. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of leukocyte depletion in PRP on proliferation and chondrogenesis of synovium-derived MSCs (SD- MSCs) and chondrocytes. METHODS: Preparation of PPP, P-PRP, L-PRP : From donated human fresh blood, we prepared three formulations of PRP: (1) platelet-poor plasma (PPP), (2) PRP with a very few leukocytes (P-PRP) and (3) PRP with high concentrations of both platelets and leukocytes (L-PRP). PPP is the upper layer of plasma after centrifuging of lOcc whole blood at 2400rpm lOmin. After 2nd centrifiiging at 3600rpm 15min, P-PRP is the lower layer of plasma without buffy coat. L-PRP is the lower layer of plasma with buffy coat. To perform the activation, we mixed thrombin powder 135 U/ml and calcium chloride 14 mg/ml. Primary cell culture and in-vitro expansion: From synovial tissues and cartilage from knee joint undergoing total knee arthroplasty, human SD-MSCs and chondrocyte were obtained by enzyme digestion. The primary cells were expanded in DMEM media with 3 formulations of PRPs. The cell proliferation was measured using the MTT assay. We used passage 2 cells for following experiments. Chondrogenesis: Chondrogenic differentiation of SD-MSCs and expanded chondrocytes were induced using a high-density pellet culture system. Aliquots of 5xl05cells were centrifuged at 500 g for 5 min, which were subsequently cultured for 3 weeks. The pellets of SD-MSCs and chondrocytes were cultured in chemically defined chondrogenic medium with 10 ng/ml TGF-pi and/or 100 ng/ml BMP-2. The medium was changed every other day. Real-time PCR: Total RNA from SD-MSCs and chondrocytes were extracted by using the RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen). Expressions of chondrogenesis factors (Type II collagen, Type X collagen, Aggrecan, Sox9) were analyzed by RT-PCR. Expression of GAPDH was taken as internal control. Histologic and Immunohistochemical Examination: Pellets were stained with Safranin-O for proteoglycan detection. The expression of type II collagen was detected by immunohistochemical staining and was observed under microscopy. RESULTS SECTION: Leukocyte depletion also lowered the count of platelets. L-PRP showed more proliferative effect on SD-MSCs and chondrocytes than P-PRP (Fig. 2). RT-PCR revealed higher cartilage gene expression in TGF-pi induced chondrogenesis of SD-MSCs and chondrocytes with P-PRP. However, there was negative effect of both formulations in TGF-pi/BMP induced chondrogenesis. In TGF-pi and/or BMP induced chondrogenesis, the SD-MSC pellet with P-PRP showed more proteoglycan production than those with L-PRP. And, type II collagen synthesis in the chondrocyte pellets with P-PRP was greater than the pellets with L-PRP. However, type II collagen synthesis in SD-MSCs pellets was not detected. DISCUSSION: Although leukocyte depletion in PRP showed negative effect on proliferation of SD-MSCs and chondrocytes, and positive effect on the mRNA expression of the chondrogenic differentiation marker genes, it could not change the negative effects of PRP on chondrogenic differentiation of SD-MSCs. SIGNIFICANCE: The results of this study would contribute to found the ideal formulations of PRP for the cartilage repairs.

title: Evaluation of a surrogate contact model of TKA
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Simultaneous prediction of body-level dynamics and detailed joint mechanics in the frame of musculoskeletal (MS) modeling represents still a highly computationally demanding task. Marra et al. (2014) recently presented and validated a MS model capable of concurrent prediction of muscle forces, knee ligament forces, tibiofemoral (TF) and patellofemoral (PF) contact forces in a MS model of Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA) [1]. Simulation time for one complete gait cycle was in the order of 3 hours, and the iterative process that solved the equilibrium in the knee joint was thought to be the main source of overhead. Surrogate modeling techniques were suggested [2]. In this study, we develop a surrogate contact model of TKA to decrease the simulation time in the MS simulation. We hypothesize that the algorithm that allows the muscle fibers to wrap around the bones constitutes another source of overhead in the MS model. Therefore, we will also evaluate the performances of the surrogate model with and without muscle wrapping. METHODS: The original tibial component from our TKA model [1] was split in a medial and lateral hemi-part and fixed to the ground, whereas the femoral part was left with 6 degrees of freedom (DOF). The contacting pairs exchanged three forces and three moments, which were assumed functions of the relative pose only. Translations (X, Y, Z) were defined relative to the tibial component frame and rotations of the femoral component (RotX, RotY, RotZ) were described with Cardan angles, using the z-y-x rotation sequence. Similarly to Lin et al (2010) [3] we identified two sensitive directions, Y and RotX and, therefore, we defined a sample point as composed by four pose parameters and the two loads in the sensitive directions: X, Fy, Z, Tx, RotY, RotZ. Reference load-pose data were obtained from four simulations of gait, squat, chair-rise, and right-turn trials using the original contact model. The design space was populated using the Hammersley quasi-random sequence and adopting a multi-domain approach, as proposed by Eskinazi and Fregly (2015) [2]. One domain consisted of 20 data points per each frame of the four dynamic simulations, spanning the boundaries of ± 1 standard deviation from the time-varying reference envelopes. A second domain of 2500 points was generated in the principal component space of the reference load-pose data of each dynamic simulation, with boundaries enlarged by 50%. A third domain of 1000 data points represented one-side-contact situations, in which Tx was bounded to ± 4 Nm. In total, 36000 data points were sampled in the three different domains. Data points were evaluated using the original contact model (Fig. 1) by repeated Force-Dependent Kinematics (FDK) analyses. Data points which did not lead to equilibrium were discarded. The remaining 27620 points were randomly subdivided into a training (70%) and testing (30%) group. Three separate Feed-Forward Artificial Neural Networks (FFANN), consisting of four inner layers of 20 hyperbolic tangent sigmoid neurons each, were configured within the Neural Network Toolbox in MATLAB 8.1 (The Math Works Inc., Natick, MA, 2013). The first network was trained to learn the relationships between the four-two medial and two lateral- sensitive loads (output) and the six pose parameters (input). Two other networks -one medial and one lateral- were trained separately to learn the relationships between the remaining loads of each side (output) and all the pose parameters plus the two sensitive loads from each side (input). We used the popular Levenberg-Marquardt training algorithm in conjunction with Bayesian regularization to avoid over-fitting. Stopping criterion was a training time of two hours for each network. The trained networks were translated to custom C++ DLL functions for successive inclusion in our MS model. The surrogate contact model replaced the original contact model and one gait trial was simulated with 4 different combination of the following model settings: original versus surrogate contact model, wrapping enabled versus disabled. RESULTS: The contact sampling model required 238 hours to evaluate the 36000 data points. Predicted tibiofemoral compressive forces under all simulated cases are shown in Fig. 2. A comparison with experimental measurements (eTibia line) is also shown. Surrogate model predictions showed a very good agreement with the original model counterparts. Fig. 3 summarizes the computation times: simulations took the longest when muscle wrapping was enabled and the benefits of using the surrogate model became evident only when the wrapping algorithm was switched off, leading to a 6x speed-up. Simulation time with the original contact model decreased by a factor of 8 by switching off the wrapping algorithm. DISCUSSION: The use of FFANN-based surrogate contact model, in place of the original rigid contact model, could substantially reduce the simulation time of a full gait cycle down to 3 minutes, when the wrapping algorithm was turned off. Such improvement could not be achieved when using the wrapping algorithm. This enlightens another important source of overhead in MS modeling -the muscle wrapping algorithm- which unexpectedly was found to dominate the simulation time. At each FDK iteration, the wrapping algorithm needs to be solved as well, introducing overhead. If the wrapping algorithm is slower than the contact algorithm, then the computation time of each step will be dominated by the former, leaving only a small fraction to be gained from the latter. SIGNIFICANCE: We showed that surrogate contact model could reduce the simulation time in a MS model of TKA down to a level which allows parametric studies and/or optimization to be feasible. We also discovered that the muscle wrapping algorithm constituted an unexpectedly large source of overhead during dynamic simulations. These represent new and important findings for the MS modeling community.

title: Combination therapy with BMP-2 and a systemic RANKL inhibitor enhances bone healing in a mouse critical-sized femoral defect
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Although recombinant human BMP-2 (rhBMP-2) is the most potent osteoinductive agent available, there are potential limitations regarding its efficacy in clinical scenarios, since it can stimulate not only bone formation, but also osteoclastogenesis with premature bone resorption. [13] Combination therapy with an anti-osteoclastic agent could potentially serve to optimize the osteoinductive activity of BMP-2 and further enhance bone healing. Osteoprotegerin (OPG) is a RANKL inhibitor that blocks differentiation and function of osteoclasts and subsequent bone resorption. It reduces osteoclast numbers to barely-detectable levels thus allowing histomorphometric analysis to succinctly indicate the degree of resorption inhibition. Therefore OPG-Fc is an excellent tool to evaluate the bone repair potential of rhBMP-2 combined with osteoclast inhibition. In the present study we hypothesized that the combination of local BMP-2 (recombinant protein or a product of gene therapy) plus systemic OPG-Fc is more effective than BMP-2 alone in promoting bone repair. It has also been shown that cells transduced with a lentivirus expressing BMP-2 exhibit a sustained (up to 12 weeks) low-level release of BMP-2.[4] We used this construct to test the secondary hypothesis that the prolonged BMP release associated with gene therapy would blunt the osteoclastic activation, such that the positive impact of OPG on bone repair would be less significant in the gene therapy group than the recombinant BMP group. Methods: This animal protocol was reviewed and approved by IACUC before the commencement of any animal studies. 156 male, transgenic mice expressing Col2.3eGFP were used for the study. An externally stabilized, critical-sized femoral defect was created using a well-established model.[3] The animals were randomly assigned to one of the following groups: rhBMP-2 (group I); rhBMP-2 and systemic OPG (group II); rhBMP-2 and delayed administration of OPG (group III); mouse bone marrow cells (MBMC) transduced with a lentiviral vector containing the BMP-2 gene (LV-BMP-2; group IV); LV-BMP-2 transduced MBMC and systemic OPG (group V); a collagen sponge alone (group VI); and OPG alone (group VII). Both the rhBMP-2 and the transduced MBMSCs were delivered on a collagen sponge. All of the animals received weekly subcutaneous injections of OPG (15mg/kg) or 0.9% NaCl (groups I, IV and VI), until euthanasia at 56 days. In the continuous administration groups, weekly OPG injections began on the first post-operative day. In the delayed administration group, mice started receiving OPG injections 2 weeks after the surgical procedure. Mice were euthanized at 7, 14, 28 and 56 days post-operatively. Bone healing was assessed with radiographs, microCT, regular (H&E and TRAP) and frozen histology and quantitative histomorphometry. Results: All bone defects treated with BMP-2 (alone or combined with OPG) were considered completely healed at the 28- and 56-day time points, whereas minimal bone formation was noted in animals treated with the carrier alone or OPG alone (Figure 1). MicroCT analysis revealed a thicker cortex in groups treated with a combination of BMP-2 and OPG (Figure 2). Post scanning analysis of defects showed that bone volume (BV) in the rhBMP-2+OPG (3.47 ± 1.37 mm3) and the LV-BMP-2+OPG (3.40 ± 0.52 mm3) groups was significantly higher compared to rhBMP-2 alone (1.71 ± 0.63 mm3, pO.Ol) and LV-BMP-2 alone (1.08 ±0.27 mm3, pO.OOl). The histomorphometric analysis revealed similar results, with rhBMP-2 alone defects exhibiting significantly lower BV compared to rhBMP-2+OPG defects (1.77±0.49mm3 vs 3.72±1.62mm3, p=0.002) and LV-BMP-2 defects (1 ± 0.32mm3) having a significantly lower BV compared to all BMP-2+OPG treated groups (p<0.01). No difference was observed between the three BMP-2+OPG groups with respect to microCT and histomorphometry. TRAP staining demonstrated a major osteoclast response in the groups that did not receive OPG (rhBMP-2, LV-BMP-2 and sponge alone) beginning as early as 7 days post operatively and reaching a peak at 14 to 28 days. This osteoclastic response was associated with bone resorption and thinning of the bony bridge in the BMP-2 alone groups at the later time points. In contrast, minimal TRAP+ cells were detected at all time points in the OPG treated groups, an effect that was associated with more robust bone formation. Discussion: This study demonstrated that the combination of locally delivered BMP-2, in the form of either recombinant protein or gene therapy, combined with systemically administered OPG can improve bone healing compared to rhBMP-2 alone or gene therapy alone in a mouse critical-sized bone defect. In the BMP only treatment groups a vigorous local osteoclastic activation was noted and was associated with resorption of newly formed bone, thereby diminishing the total volume of bone induced in the defect. No difference was observed with respect to osteoclast activation and subsequent osteolysis between rhBMP-2 and LV-BMP-2 gene therapy, despite the difference in the release profile between the two. This suggests that the presence of BMP-2 alone, regardless of the pattern of exposure, can lead to stimulation of osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption at the site of implantation. Administration of OPG reduced osteoclasts to barely detectable levels, an effect that was consistently associated with improvements in bone volume. SIGNIFICANCE: In order to optimize BMP-induced bone healing it may be necessary to modulate BMP's effect on osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption, by combining it with an anti-osteoclastic agent. In this study we demonstrated that the combination of systemic OPG-Fc and local BMP-2 leads to enhanced bone repair in a femoral defect by preventing the premature resorption of newly formed bone. RANKL inhibitors could be potentially used as adjuvants in challenging bone healing scenarios as they can be easily administered via a subcutaneous injection in an outpatient setting following surgical intervention. References: [l]Seeherman HJ et al. RhBMP-2 induces transient bone resorption followed by bone formation in a nonhuman primate core-defect model. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2010; 92:411-26. [2]Toth JM et al. Short-term Osteoclastic Activity Induced by Locally High Concentrations of Recombinant Human Bone Morphogenetic Protein-2 in a Cancellous Bone Environment. Spine. 2009;34:539-50. [3]Alaee F et al. Evaluation of osteogenic cell differentiation in response to bone morphogenetic protein or demineralized bone matrix in a critical sized defect model using GFP reporter mice. J Orthop Res. 2014;32:1120-28. [4]Feeley BT et al. In vivo molecular imaging of adenoviral versus lentiviral gene therapy in two bone formation models. J Orthop Res. 2006;24:1709-21.

title: Microscopic MR imaging and polarized light microscopy of hypertrophic articular cartilage
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Articular cartilage (AC), the soft connective tissue covering the ends of bones in articulating joints, is a matrix consisting of collagen fibers, proteoglycan macromolecules, and sparsely spaced cells (chondrocytes). From the articular surface (AS) to the cartilage-bone interface (tidemark; TM), normal articular cartilage can be divided into a superficial zone (SZ), transitional zone (TZ), and radial zone (RZ) where collagen fibers are oriented parallel, random, and perpendicular to the AS, respectively. When the AS is oriented perpendicular (0° reference) to the external magnetic field (B0) the nuclear dipolar interaction and anisotropic orientation of collagen fibers cause T2 images to appear laminar and T2 profiles to exhibit a bell-shape curve. The T2 profiles can be used for zonal classification of articular cartilage. Polarized light microscopy (PLM) has the ability to measure collagen fiber organization and density. Those PLM measurements are comparable to the T2@0° images since fiber organization and density contribute to the laminar appearance seen in μMRI. Therefore, PLM can be used to describe characteristics seen in μMRI T2 weighted images. There is an additional benefit in PLM such that we can image chondrocytes and assess hypertrophy characteristics caused by disease such as osteoarthritis (OA). Degenerative diseases such as OA can alter the normal structure of articular cartilage and can present in many forms, including chondrocyte hypertrophy. Since this abnormality can alter what we see from imaging techniques, the objective of this study is to compare hypertrophic features seen in high-resolution MR images and polarized light microscopy. METHODS: Three canines underwent anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) transection in one knee, then sacrificed 25 weeks post-operation. An additional canine did not undergo operation and was used as a control. Animal care approved by a review board (CCAC). For each transected knee joint, a block approximately 6mm x 2.6mm (anterior-posterior axis; medial-lateral axis, respectively) was cut from the central load-bearing region of the medial tibial condyle. Each block was imaged using μMRI and PLM. The tissue blocks were never frozen prior to MRI. T2 weighted μMRI was performed on a Bruker Ascend 300WB 7T/89mm vertical bore superconducting magnet. Samples were soaked overnight in a ImM Gd(DTPA)2 solution (Magnevist, NJ), then sealed in glass MR tubes (Wilmad Glass, NJ) and oriented in the magnet with the AS perpendicular to the external B0 field (0° orientation). Imaging was performed using five delay times (2ms, 8ms, 20ms, 40ms, 70ms), a 256 x 128 acquisition matrix (reconstructed to a 256 x 256 matrix), and 4.5mm x 4.5mm field-of-view (FOV), which yielded 17.6 μm pixel resolution. Slice selection was taken through the center of the block (coronal axis). Regions of interest (ROI)10 columns wide were used in T2@0° profile calculations. The tissue blocks were fixated in a 10% formal-CPC solution for approximately 24 hours then frozen in water and microtomed into 6 μm full thickness slices using a Leica CM1950 cryostat. Microtomed sections were taken at the same location as the MRI slice. PLM imaging was performed on a Leica DMRX microscope equipped with a CRI Abrio polarized light imaging system. Images were taken using 5x objective magnification yielding 2.5 μm pixel resolution. The resulting images were used to qualitatively compare μMRI features with chondrocyte and cartilage matrix features. RESULTS: The control sample T2 image, PLM image, and T2 profile (Fig. 1) show the well-known features of healthy articular cartilage. The T2 image (Fig. la) has a laminar appearance with a low intensity superficial zone, high intensity transitional zone, and low intensity radial zone. The T2 profile has a typical bell-shape curve, where the peak values (maximum at approximately 70 ms) indicate the transitional zone of collagen fibers. The PLM image has a similar laminar appearance, with intensities opposite that of μMRI. The chondrocytes are well organized with elongation parallel and perpendicular to the AS in the SZ and RZ, respectively. Hypertrophied cartilage shows distinctively different features (Fig. 2). In the T2 images, several additional laminae are visible below the AS in two samples (Fig. 2a,c) and a significant thickness increase occurs in the SZ of one sample (Fig. 2e). The T2 profiles (Fig. 3) show the additional lamina as a second peak occurring deeper in the tissue. Additionally, the maximum T2 value increased to approximately 90-100ms. The PLM retardation images show the characteristics causing the T2 variation. In fig 2b and 2d, there appears to be residual features of a SZ with chondrocytes parallel to the AS beneath a hypertrophied zone. This feature is most prominent in fig 2d. There is no residual feature of a typical SZ in fig 2f, which shows significant SZ hypertrophy. DISCUSSION: The first bell-shape curve in fig 3a and 3b have a leading segment that is typical of a SZ. In contrast, PLM images do not show atypical SZ zone, and instead show what may be a thin highly organized or dense surface layer covering a hypertrophied zone. The high-density or well-organized surface is also seen in the μMRI images (Fig. 2a,c). A high-density layer may be a protective layer for the soft hypertrophied tissue. A zone more closely related to a typical transitional zone occurs at the secondary peak. The chondrocytes do not appear to have the same degree of hypertrophy as those in the zone defined by the first peak. The increase in T2 values may be caused by hypertrophic chondrocytes since they contain greater amounts of free water. It appears that various stages of hypertrophy are present in these cartilage samples. In fig 2d, there is a well-defined lamina (high-intensity line) through the entire sample width, covered by a hypertrophied zone. The residual SZ in fig 2b was present only on the left side of the cartilage block and a transition to severe hypertrophy occurred toward the right side of the cartilage block. The lack of a typical SZ in fig 2f may show an end-stage of hypertrophic reaction. High intensity edges were present in the PLM image, possibly from freezing prior to microtomy. Although the edges cannot be used in PLM analysis, the hypertrophic regions were unaffected. The μMRI images do not show the entire FOV since the cartilage and bone region was enlarged to show detail. By enlarging the desired regions, an interference line artifact at the bottom of the raw T2 images is not shown. The line did not transect the cartilage and had no effect on cartilage T2 values. SIGNIFICANCE: High-resolution MRI provides insight into hypertrophied cartilage. Knowing the causes and effects of hypertrophy on T2 images may allow for non-invasive in vivo assessment of OA treatment efficacy and diagnosis.

title: Novel modifications for enhancement of femoral segmental defect atrophic non-union mouse model
abstract: INTRODUCTION: It is estimated that 100,000 fractures in the United States will progress to non-union each year1. Even with improved healing strategies and external fixation devices, the overall rate of fracture complications has not been significantly reduced. Atrophic non-union is defined as a non-union with sparse or no evidence of callus formation. This subtype is particularly challenging to treat because, rather than a mechanical problem, it is viewed as a biological problem. While the pathophysiological mechanisms are largely unknown, incidence of atrophic non-union is multi-factorial. It may be avascular and requires a bone graft in addition to fixation. However, bone grafts readily fail and cause donor site morbidity, while fixation will not cause union to be achieved if the fracture has become atrophic and osteoporotic. Atrophic non-union is associated with a prolonged treatment schedule, resulting in pain, functional, and psychological disability. Creation of segmental defect in preclinical models is likely the best approach for mimicking the clinical situation of impaired healing, as it can be readily standardized and easily allows for analysis of the effects of scaffolding, cell transplantation, and implantation of osteogenic factors at the defect site. Pre-clinical models for non-union have been described in rodents, rabbits, and sheep. In regard to mouse models of atrophic non-union, the LockingMouseNail kit (RISystems) provides a highly standardized approach in which stabilized segmental defects are achieved through interlocked intramedullary nailing. In this study, we developed novel modifications that allowed for 1) a completely aseptic surgical environment and 2) a reduction in fracture gap size that redefines critical size gap defect when using the LockingMouseNail kit. METHODS: This study was conducted using male C57B1/6 mice and all procedures were conducted under approved Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee protocols. Cefazolin (lOmg/ml; lOOul volume), a first generation cephalosporin, and Buprenorphine (0.03mg/mL in lOOul volume), an analgesic, were administered subcutaneously 45 minutes prior to surgery. Mice were anesthetized and the surgical site prepared under sterile conditions (shaving of the surgical area followed by betadine and 70% ethanol scrub). The mouse was then positioned on a heating pad and wrapped in Press 'n' Seal (Glad), leaving the prepared surgical area exposed. The leg was then prepared by a sterile hanging leg preparation using sterile PetFlex (Andover). A surgical drape was placed over the top of the surgical area. A longitudinal incision was made along the dorsal surface of the knee and the patella was dislocated laterally to expose the knee joint. The epicondyle of the femur was then opened using a centering drill bit and the marrow cavity was reamed using a 22G blunted stainless steel needle. A 27G needle was used to open the femur proximally. The MouseNail was then inserted into the marrow cavity under continuous manual rotation until the distal end was flush with the epicondyle. The aiming device of the MouseNail was then positioned to allow for insertion of interlocking pins. Holes for the pins were generated with countersinking and 1 locking pin was inserted on each side of the fracture gap to be created. The aiming device was then removed from the MouseNail. Osteotomy was created using a sterile Dremel bit to generate a fracture gap of 1.6 mm. Care was taken to keep the periosteum intact. The shaft of the MouseNail protruding from the epicondyle region was then disconnected with a Dremel saw to allow the nail to be completely flush with the epicondyle. We first covered this area with Vaseline to prevent metal shrapnel from infiltrating the soft tissue, which could have led to inflammation. The patellar tendon/patella was then re-positioned. The skin was sutured closed using absorbable sutures and Tissumend II synthetic tissue adhesive. Buprenorphine (0.03mg/mL in lOOul volume) was administered subcutaneously 4 hours after surgery. Mice were monitored daily for signs of inflammation, discomfort, or inability to ambulate. Mice were examined by micro-CT at 6 time points post-surgery (Id, 7d, 14d, 28d, 56d, 70d) to ensure lack of callus formation or bridging of the fracture gap, thus confirming successful generation of atrophic non-union. RESULTS: Methods developed to establish a sterile surgical field resulted in all animals surviving the operation without any evidence of early complications due to bone or soft tissue infection. One animal was euthanized 48 hours post-operation due to fracture of the lateral femoral condyle. Our findings show that the use of Press 'n' Seal results in maintenance of sterility across the entire surgical field. The development of a method for a hanging leg preparation allowed the leg to be maneuvered throughout the surgery, resulting in increased precision of entry into the medullary cavity, without compromising sterility. Together, these refinements led to a standardized, cost-effective method for establishing an aseptic surgical environment for murine orthopedic studies. Using this method, we then created a 1.6 mm osteotomy in a cohort of C57B1/6 animals (n=4). Micro-CT analysis of fracture gap demonstrated the absence of callus formation and gap bridging in all animals past the time of normal healing (4 weeks) and up to ten weeks post-operation. These results indicate that a fracture gap size of 1.6 mm results in successful generation of atrophic non-union. Ongoing longitudinal studies will continue to monitor these studies to the 12 week post-operative time point, at which time, animals will be subjected to high resolution ex vivo micro-CT analysis. DISCUSSION: The adaptation of preclinical non-union studies to the mouse model allows for more elegant mechanistic studies through the use of transgenic and genetic animal models not available in larger species. The LockingMouseNail kit results in rigid fixation of a defined fracture gap using locking pins that fit through the intramedullary nail, thereby limiting micro-motion and movement of the fracture ends. This approach reliably generated atrophic non-union in CD-I mice2. Studies have shown that reliable generation of fractures is dependent on mouse strain used, with C57B1/6 demonstrating a rapid healing rate3. Given the widespread use of this strain, standardized methods for generation of non-union are important toward elucidating the mechanisms regulating non-union healing. In our study, we have generated atrophic non-union in a cohort of C57B1/6 mice using aseptic methods in conjunction with modifications to this LockingMouseNail system. In previous murine studies, atrophic non-union has been achieved with a fracture gap size of 2.0 mm using the LockingMouseNail kit (RISystems). However, for development of orthopedic treatment strategies, it is vital to generate atrophic nonunion with a critical gap size defect that can be healed upon intervention. Our findings suggest that atrophic non-union can be reliably achieved with a standard gap size of 1.6 mm. Together, the novel modifications developed in this study can be applied to increase reproducibility of the technically challenging surgery, understand the basic mechanisms of non-union fracture repair, and utilize this knowledge to examine the efficacy of clinically relevant therapeutics. Our laboratory is interested in using the novel model developed herein to examine the ability of stem cells to prevent atrophic non-union formation. SIGNIFICANCE: We have generated atrophic non-union in a mouse model using aseptic technique for the entirety of the procedure, which more readily mimics human surgery and mitigates the possibility for infection, which could complicate study results. Atrophic non-union is still difficult to treat clinically, thus the need to develop novel treatment strategies in appropriate precise and reproducible models, such as the one we have developed.

title: The role of osteoactivin in bone regeneration: a sheep model for cancellous bone healing
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The search for osteoinductive therapeutic compounds remains critical to help accelerate bone healing in the case of major bone trauma, osteoporotic fractures, fusion surgeries, delayed or nonunions, revision prosthetic surgeries, and several oncology cases. Autologous bone grafting is most commonly used for the treatment of these cases and as such is the second most frequent tissue transplantation worldwide, second only to blood transfusions, with over 2 million bone grafting procedures performed each year worldwide. However, despite this high frequency autologous bone grafting has many disadvantages and inherit morbidity secondary to surgical donor site pain, blood loss, hematoma formation, infection, injury to local structure s, and longer operative times. Also, bone graft availability may be limited in select populations especially in pediatric and elderly patients. Several models have been introduced and well documented to study osteoinductive compounds and biomaterials in bone healing. Osteoactivin (OA) is an osteoinductive protein encoded by the GPNMB gene that has previously been shown by our group to stimulate osteoblast differentiation and function in vitro and bone regeneration in vivo. Our lab has shown that Osteoactivin expression is increased during fracture healing and in a rat model of bone marrow ablation. In order to demonstrate therapeutic efficacy of OA in bone regeneration, a larger animal model is necessary to predict the effect of the compound in humans. Thus, the sheep model provides a way to study the effect of OA on osteogenesis by inducing critical size defects into the long bones of the animals. In this study, we show that critical size defects introduced into bilateral distal femurs of a sheep (n=6) dosed with an O A-soaked absorbable collagen sponge had significantly accelerated bone healing and regeneration, characterized by radiographic, uCT imaging and histological analysis when compared to control sheep (defect only or collagen sponge treated alone). METHODS: Approval of the Northeast Ohio Medical University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) was obtained prior to the start of this study. Six (6) male sheep (Ovis aries) between ages 2-3 years old were used, each with a critical size defect (25 mm in depth x 11 mm in diameter) drilled into bilateral hind limb distal femurs. The surgical protocol utilized was based on previous work done to develop a model for cancellous bone healing (Malhotra et al, 2014). This method allowed for high quality standardization and sterility processes across each sheep. Furthermore, Martini et al, 2001 and Pearce et al, 2007 have demonstrated comparable rates of bone healing, bone turnover, and remodeling activity between sheep and humans. The procedures were performed by an orthopedic surgeon. Once under appropriate anesthesia, one femur defect (left hindlimb) was drilled with a cannulated acorn drill (Stryker) and packed with an PBS absorbable collagen sponge (Medline Industries) without OA protein and thus functioned as a control, while the other defect (right hindlimb) was filled with either a low dose (10 ug), or high dose (50 ug) recombinant OA-soaked collagen sponge (R&D Systems). Three sheep received the high dose OA while two received the low dose OA, and one was left as a control. The animals were allowed to recover and then terminated after a period of 10 weeks. The femurs were harvested for x-ray (General Electric) and uCT (Scanco) imaging. Blood and urine samples were collected for CBC, CMP and urinalysis (ANTECH Diagnostics). Tissue biopsies were taken from heart, lung, liver, spleen, kidney, thyroid gland, adrenal gland, and skeletal muscle for RNA and histological analyses during post-mortem dissection. RESULTS: Initial radiographic analysis indicated a complete regeneration of bone at the defect site in both high-dose and low-dose treated sheep, while the control femurs showed no significant change in the size ofthe defect or significant bone regeneration (see Figure 1). Micro-CT analysis of control and OA-treated defects measured the bone volume and density ofthe regenerated area indicating a significant increase at the OA-treated defect sites (see Figure 2). CBC, CMP and urinalysis showed no apparent abnormalities between control and OA-treated sheep. DISCUSSION: As a result of this study, it is evident that OA plays a crucial role in bone remodeling and growth following injury in a large animal model. This provides a proof of concept that O A can potentially be utilized as a therapeutic target in accelerating b one regrowth following traumatic injury. Further studies are underway to determine dosing for optimum therapeutic effect and are also needed to compare OA to currently approved osteoinductive compounds such as Bone Morphogenic Protein-2 (BMP-2). Thus far OA has proven to be safe when administered locally with no apparent adverse systemic effects per laboratory studies or histological sampling ofthe sheep. Our current work indicates feasibility and cause for continued work in assessing OA as a therapeutic target for bone regeneration. SIGNIFICANCE: The study shows that OA has promising effects on bone regeneration in a large animal model and can potentially be used as a novel therapeutic agent for a wide variety of patients that would typically require bone grafting but without the inherent side effects.

title: Establishing an endothelial progenitor cell dose response for the healing of critical size bone defects
abstract: INTRODUCTION The management of bone defects and nonunions continues to represent a significant clinical challenge for orthopaedic surgeons. The current treatment for bone defects includes further surgical intervention that is often not successful at promoting any further healing. Proteins that promote bone cell differentiation, as well as the application of bone cell precursors have been investigated pre-clinically; however, these treatments have all had limited success clinically. Within recent years, our group has identified and successfully addressed the issue of insufficient blood flow to non-healing fractures with a bone marrow-derived progenitor cell: the endothelial progenitor cell (EPC). When applied locally on a collagen scaffold, we have shown that EPCs promote bone healing in non-healing rat femur fracture model. The goal of this current study is therefore to build on this past success by optimizing the amount of EPCs used for fracture healing-while also assessing their safety and efficacy. We hypothesize that the local application of EPCs to a non-healing defect will improve bone healing in a dose-dependent manner until a plateau of effectiveness is reached. METHODS Male Fischer-344 rats underwent a double osteotomy of the right femur to create a 5mm critical size defect that was then stabilized by a mini-plate and screws. Prior to surgery, varying amounts of EPCs were seeded onto a biodegradable collagen scaffold (125mm3) that was then placed into the created defect. The doses of EPCs investigated in this study were: one hundred thousand, five hundred thousand, one million, two million, and four million (n=3). The cells used for implantation were isolated from the bone marrow of a separate rat, which was then cultured in endothelial growth medium (EGM-2-MV-SingleQuots) for 7 days. Postoperative bi-weekly radiographs of the operated femur were taken up until the 10-week endpoint to evaluate the progress of healing. These radiographs were then scored by blinded assessors according to bone filling and callus density (on a scale from 0-8), and these data analyzed statistically to give Kappa values. Post-sacrifice, operated and contralateral intact femurs were evaluated with microCT (ScanCo 40, 8um voxel, 70kVp, 114|xA) to study bone volume, density, and trabecular parameters (number, thickness, and spacing). The femurs were then assessed for functionality with biomechanical testing and compared against healthy contralateral femurs. Briefly, femurs were tested in torsion (1° per second, 20mm gauge length) using an MTS Bionix 858, and their load-displacement data recorded. Torsional strength was defined as the maximum load sustained, while stiffness was defined as the slope of the load-displacement data up until the point of maximum torque. All animal protocols were approved by the St. Michael's Hospital Animal Care Committee. RESULTS Earlier bone healing and union (defined as a score of at least 7 in our scored radiographs) was observed in animals that received the 4 million EPC treatment-the largest dose in our study (Table 1). However at the 10-week endpoint, rats that received 2 millions EPCs showed the greatest bone volume formed via microCT evaluation (Figure 1). Biomechanical testing also demonstrated that rats treated with 2 million EPCs exhibited the greatest torsional strength among all treatment groups, including being significantly stronger (p<0.05) than the higher 4 million EPC dose (Figure 2). Also evident in the scored radiographic data was the less than optimal rate of union when 500,000 cells or less was applied to our femoral defect (Table 1). DISCUSSION To date, an optimal concentration of bone marrow-derived progenitor cells delivered to a bone defect to promote healing has not been defined. In this study, we demonstrate a peak of effectiveness when 2 million ex-vivo expanded EPCs are delivered locally to a 5mm femoral defect. Although not investigated here, enhanced vascularity at the site of fracture may be the reason for this peak effect, whereby our highest dose (4 million) may experience over-vascularization that precludes the formation of bone in vital areas of the defect. With bone volume being a large contributor to mechanical strength, the lack of bone in the 4 million EPC treatment group relative to the 1 and 2 million cell groups may explain its lackluster biomechanical strength. In addition, further analysis of the microarchitecture of these animals that received 4 million EPCs reveal a lower number of trabeculae than are present in the 1 and 2 million treatment groups; another nod to its mechanical underperformance. These data present a novel perspective in fracture healing and cell-delivery, showcasing a limitation of treating a bone defect with an increasing number of cells. Evidently, this unexpected result is not in line with our study's original hypothesis of a plateau of effectiveness. One limitation of the current study to keep in mind is our choice of scaffold. Although collagen scaffolds provide the radiolucency necessary analyze the early stages of healing radiographically, synthetic calcium-phosphate scaffolds can be engineered to provide the optimal osteoconductive environment for bone healing. SIGNIFICANCE Our findings demonstrate that there exists an optimal amount of autologous endothelial progenitor cells for healing of a critical size defect, dispelling the common theme that more is always better. This study brings a significant contribution to the translation of cell-therapies from small animal models to more clinically relevant large animal investigations with a method that has been optimized to promote bone healing in critical size defects.

title: Characterization of meniscus-derived matrix and evaluation for repair of the meniscus
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The menisci are fibrocartilaginous tissues that distribute loads in the knee and provide a low friction surface for joint loading. Meniscal tears, particularly those in the avascular inner zone, have a poor healing capacity. Meniscal tears are associated with cartilage degeneration and the development of osteoarthritis (1). Therefore, strategies to promote meniscus repair and induce long-term regeneration of functional meniscus tissue are needed. Extracellular matrix derived scaffolds contain the native components of the extracellular matrix and have been shown to promote cell infiltration and remodeling of the scaffold (2,3). The objective of this study was to generate meniscus-derived matrix (MDM) scaffolds and test the effectiveness of these scaffolds to promote meniscus repair in an in vitro model. Methods: Scaffold Preparation: Medial menisci were harvested from porcine knee joints (n = 33) and minced. The tissue was frozen, lyophilized, and pulverized into a fine powder. The MDM powder was suspended in deionized water at concentrations of either 4% or 8% weight/weight, and homogenized into a slurry. This slurry was placed into delrin molds (3 mm diameter x 2 mm deep), frozen at -80°C, and then lyophilized to form porous scaffolds. Half of the scaffolds were dehydrothermally crosslinked for 24 hrs at 120°C. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images were taken of the scaffolds. Meniscal Repair Model Explant Harvest and Culture: Explants (5 mm diameter x 2mm thick) were harvested from skeletally mature female porcine medial menisci. To simulate a full-thickness defect, a 3 mm diameter core was removed (4). For control samples, the core was reinserted. For experimental samples, the core was replaced with 4%, 4% crosslinked (X), 8%, or 8% X MDM scaffolds. MDM scaffolds alone (no tissue) and meniscal repair model explants containing MDM inner cores (tissue) were cultured for 28 days. Outcome Measures: Confocal microscopy and histological staining were performed after 7, 14, 21, and 28 days in culture to visualize live cells (calcein AM) and matrix (Alexa Fluor 633 NHS ester) and collagen (fast green) and proteoglycans (safranin O) respectively. After 28 days, a push-out test was performed to determine the interfacial shear strength between the outer ring and inner core (n > 5/group) (4). The MDM cores were then papain digested (n > 6/group). The papain digests were analyzed for sulfated glycosaminoglycan (sGAG) content by the DMMB assay (5), collagen content using the hydroxyproline assay (6), and DNA content using picogreen. Differences among the groups for the biochemical data were determined using a factorial ANO VA to assess the effects of MDM concentration, crosslinking, and the presence or absence of tissue. For the shear strength data, a one-way ANOVA was performed. The Fisher's LSD post-hoc test was used to assess all significant differences (a=0.05). Results: SEM images of the MDM scaffolds showed a higher porosity in the 4% scaffolds than the 8% scaffolds. Confocal images indicated that meniscal cells had filled the interface and MDM scaffolds by day 28 (Fig 1). The DNA content was significantly increased in the MDM cores surrounded by meniscal tissue compared to the MDM scaffold alone (Fig 2A). However, both percent MDM and crosslinking had no effect on the DNA content in the scaffolds. On average over the 28 days, the DNA content in the MDM scaffolds with tissue reached 67% of the DNA content in the control meniscus tissue. The 8% and 8% X scaffolds had significantly higher collagen (Fig 2B) and sGAG (Fig 2C) content than the 4% and 4% X scaffolds. Interestingly, the collagen content in the MDM scaffolds decreased when cultured with the meniscus tissue. The sGAG content in the MDM scaffolds was highest in the 8% X scaffolds that were cultured with meniscal tissue, reaching 50% of the value in the meniscus tissue. The co-culture of the MDM scaffolds and the meniscal tissue significantly increased the sGAG content in the scaffold. Crosslinking of the MDM scaffolds also promoted retention of higher sGAG content. Histological staining showed increased integration of the MDM inner core with the meniscal tissue in all experimental groups over time and the most robust proteoglycan staining was detected in the crosslinked MDM scaffolds. Finally, the 4% and 8% X scaffolds demonstrated the highest shear strength of repair, as compared to all other groups, including the control meniscus tissue (Fig 2D). Discussion: Both crosslinking and concentration of the MDM influence the biochemical content and mechanical properties, allowing us to tailor the properties of the MDM scaffolds to promote tissue repair. Meniscal cells readily migrated into the MDM and the decreased collagen content in the MDM scaffolds when cultured with the meniscal tissue suggests that the meniscal cells are able to remodel the MDM scaffolds. This high affinity of the cells for the MDM combined with their ability to remodel the scaffold is promising for the potential of MDM to integrate seamlessly into the native meniscal tissue. The higher integrative shear strength of repair in the 4% and 8% X scaffolds, as compared to the native meniscus, shows promise for the potential of the MDM in enhancing meniscal repair. SIGNIFICANCE: Meniscal tears, particularly in the avascular inner zone, do not heal well and ultimately lead to the development of osteoarthritis. The MDM scaffold provides a favorable environment for meniscal cell infiltration and enhances integrative meniscal repair. Thus, it has the potential to integrate seamlessly into meniscal lesions and promote long-term repair.

title: Kartogenin promotes the formation of fibrocartilage zone between tendon graft and bone tunnel
abstract: INTRODUCTION The normal tendon-bone junction (TBJ) is a strong structure protected by the fibrocartilage transition zone. This crucial feature allows a gradual transition of mechanical forces between tendon and bone, thus decreasing stress-concentration effects. However, after an injury the transition zone in the TBJ interface is often not formed. Also, after ACL reconstruction, patients had no fibrocartilage zone regeneration [1]. Thus it is highly desirable to restore/establish the unique protective fibrocartilage transition zone in injured TBJs and after ACL reconstruction surgery. In our pursuit for an alternate therapy to induce formation of the fibrocartilage zone we chose a small heterocyclic compound called kartogenin (KGN), which was reported to induce chondrogenic differentiation of endogenous stem cells and thus repair cartilage in mice with osteoarthritis [2]. Our studies also showed that KGN injection enhanced wound healing in injured rat TBJs by forming extensive cartilage-like tissues [3]. However, it is not known whether KGN can induce the formation of fibrocartilage transition zone between a tendon graft and bone tunnel. Therefore, in this study we examined the effect of KGN treatment on the formation of fibrocartilage transition zone on a rat tendon-bone tunnel model. METHODS Preparation of KGN and PRP - Kartogenin (KGN, Catalog No. SML0370, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) stock solution (10 mM) was prepared in DMSO. KGN stock was diluted to 100 uM with PRP to obtain the KGN+PRP solution. PRP was obtained from the blood of Sprague-Dawley rats using a two-step centrifligation method described previously [4]. Platelet concentration in PRP was measured and adjusted to 3 times over the baseline platelet concentration in whole blood. Thrombin, at the concentration of 1 kU/mL, was used as the PRP activator. Animal experiment - 27 female Sprague-Dawley rats (234∼268g) were used. A 10mm skin incision was made on the medial side of the Achilles tendon to cut the fascia longitudinally. One bundle of the Achilles tendon was resected at the distal ends near the calcaneus with proximal ends of the bundle left intact. A 1.5 mm tunnel was drilled at the distal end of tibia from posterior to anterior. The tendon was pulled through the tunnel and sutured to the anterior soft tissue with resorbable suture (Polysorb 4-0). Ankle joint was fixed at 90 degrees. The skin was closed with resorbable sutures. Immediately after the procedure the rats were randomized into three groups: Group A received 50ul KGN + PRP + 5ul thrombin into the tendon-bone tunnel interface; Group B was given only 50ul PRP + 5ul thrombin; and Group C was left untreated. Histological analysis - From each group, tendon samples were dissected out from 3 rats at each of the 3 time-points (4, 8 and 12 weeks) for histological analyses. The whole tibia with the inserted tendon was harvested, fixed in 10% formalin for 24 hrs at room temperature and decalcified in 10% EDTA. Decalcification was verified in specimens by needle testing until they were free of calcium. Then, the tissues were embedded in paraffin and sectioned to 6 um thickness in the sagittal plane. Finally, the sections were stained with Safranin O and Fast green, immunostained for collagen types 1 (Col-1) and 2 (Col-2) and observed through a microscope. RESULTS All animals were in good condition after surgery and complications were not present. Safranin O staining was higher in the KGN+PRP group than the other groups indicating the regeneration of more cartilage-like transition zone in this group (Fig. 1A-C). Moreover, the density of this cartilage-like tissue was time dependent; i.e., it increased with increase in healing time. In contrast, both PRP (Fig. 1D-F) and control (Fig. 1G-I) groups had no cartilage-like tissues (Fig. 1D-I). In fact, some gaps were observed in the control group after 4 and 8 weeks (Fig. 1G-I). Finally, the cartilage-like transition zone in the KGN+PRP group also stained positive for both Col-1 and Col-2 corroborating that these were indeed fibrocartilage tissues (Fig. 2). DISCUSSION Enhancing the tendon-bone tunnel healing is a significant challenge to physicians much like ACL reconstruction. Using an animal tendon-bone tunnel injury model, we showed here that KGN promotes the formation of fibrocartilage-like transition zone between the tendon graft and bone tunnel. Thus, KGN not only promotes the formation of cartilage-like tissues but also augments regeneration of the fibrocartilage transition zone in a time-dependent manner. The unique advantage of KGN over other tissue engineering approaches used to heal the TBJ interface is that KGN application can be a method for cell-free therapy. While PRP in this study does not promote fibrocartilage formation in its own right, it functions as an effective carrier that supplies a fibrin gel scaffold and growth factors necessary to enhance wound healing. Future research is aimed to determine the optimal KGN dosage regimens and the optimal delivery method (e.g. injection of KGN+PRP vs. implantation of KGN+PRP gel) to regenerate the fibrocartilage transition zone. SIGNIFICANCE Application of KGN can be a convenient cell-free therapy that may be used with ease in clinics to enhance regeneration of the fibrocartilage transition zone in ACL reconstruction.

title: Transplantation of foxc2-transfected bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells for experimental femoral head necrosis in rabbits
abstract: BACKGROUND: Core decompression can delay early osteonecrosis of the femoral head, but cannot completely repair the necrotic femoral head. Eventually, femoral head collapse, even bone necrosis, will occur. OBJECTIVE: To explore the curative effect of implantation of gelatin sponge carrying Foxc2-transfected bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells on the repair of experimental femoral head necrosis in rabbits. METHODS: Forty New Zealand white rabbits were selected, and femoral head necrosis models were prepared successfully in 24 of 40 rabbits. Then, model rabbits were randomized into four groups: blank control group (n=4) with no treatment, core decompression group (n=4), GFP group (n=8) subjected to core decompression and implantation of gelatin sponge carrying GFP-transfected bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, and Foxc2 group (n=8) subjected to core decompression and implantation of gelatin sponge carrying Foxc2-transfected bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. At 1, 2, 4 weeks after implantation, ELISA was used to detect Foxc2 protein levels in the transplanted region. At 4, 8, 12 weeks after implantation, MRI scan of the hip was performed, and femoral head tissues were taken and sliced into sections for hematoxylin-eosin staining to observe bone growth. At 12 weeks after implantation, histomorphometry measurement and transmission electron microscope observation were carried out. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION: At 1, 2, 4 weeks after implantation, Foxc2 was highly expressed in the femoral head in the Foxc2 group, which was significantly higher than that in the GFP group. At 4, 8, 12 weeks, only a few of new bone formed in the core decompression group and GFP group; at 12 weeks, fibrous tissues formed in the decompression channel. New bone formation was evident in the Foxc2 group, and at 12 weeks, the necrotic region was repaired completely. MRI findings showed normal femoral head morphology and signals in the Foxc2 group at 12 weeks, but there were decreased signals of the femoral head in the core decompression group and GFP group. These findings indicate that Foxc2-transfected bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell transplantation via core decompression has good curative effects on experimental femoral head necrosis in animals.

title: Effects of low intensity pulsed ultrasound on the expression of type II collagen and matrix metalloproteinase-13 in chondrocytes of a rabbit model of knee arthritis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Low intensity pulsed ultrasound is safe, non-invasive, and has strong penetration. In recent years, more and more studies have indicated that low intensity pulsed ultrasound has important role in promoting the repair of damaged articular cartilage. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effect of low intensity pulsed ultrasound on the expression of type II collagen and matrix metalloproteinase 13 in articular cartilage of rabbits of knee arthritis. METHODS: A total of 20 New Zealand white rabbits were included in this study to establish knee arthritis model. All models were randomly divided into control group and experimental group, 10 rats in each group. In the experimental group, the right knee joint received low intensity pulsed ultrasound treatment with an ultrasonic fracture healing instrument. In the control group, right knee joint received false low intensity pulsed ultrasound therapy. At 8 weeks after intervention, cartilage tissue was collected from medial end of tibia and medial end of femur. After conventional treatment, toluidine blue staining was performed. Pathological observation was conducted under a microscope. Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction was used to detect matrix metalloproteinase 13 and type II collagen expression in chondrocytes. The general situation of the experimental animals was observed. The results of articular cartilage and the quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction results of matrix metalloproteinase-13 and type II collagen were observed under a microscope. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION: (1) Toluidine blue staining and pathological observation: 8 weeks after treatment, obvious fissure appeared in articular cartilages, and extending from the surface to the deep layer in the control group, and there was a lack of staining. In the experimental group, cracks formed on articular cartilage surface, and there was a moderate staining missing. (2) Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction: at 5 and 10 days after culture, significant differences in gene expression of matrix metalloproteinase-13 and type II collagen were detected at various time points in the experimental and control groups (P < 0.05). (3) The results showed that the low intensity pulsed ultrasound could affect the gene expression of matrix metalloproteinase-13 and type II collagen in the rabbit model of knee arthritis.

title: Clinical outcomes of intra-articular route versus intravenous route of tranexamic acid during total knee arthroplasty: A meta-analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tranexamic acid administered either in intra-articular route or in intravenous route can significantly reduce blood loss during total knee arthroplasty. Recent studies are still controversial in application mode of tranexamic acid in the clinic. OBJECTIVE: To compare the clinical outcomes of tranexamic acid in intra-articular route and intravenous route during total knee arthroplasty. METHODS: PubMed, OVID, Web of Science, and EMBASE were searched to identify randomized controlled trials concerning the comparison of tranexamic acid in intra-articular route and intravenous route during total knee arthroplasty published before 1 May 2015. Transfusion rate, hemoglobin decline, drainage volume and thromboembolic complication rate were considered as indexes to evaluate the clinical effect, for meta-analysis. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION: Six randomized controlled trials involving 847 patients were included. Meta-analysis results showed no significant difference between intra-articular and intravenous administration of tranexamic acid in terms of transfusion rate, hemoglobin decline, drainage volume, total blood loss, and thromboembolic complication rate. Subgroup analysis for dose regimen showed that when occlusion time of drainage tube was < 2 hours. Intra-articular route of tranexamic acid showed high drainage volume and hemoglobin decline compared with the intravenous route of tranexamic acid (P < 0.01). Results confirmed that during total knee arthroplasty, clinical effects of intra-articular and intravenous routes of tranexamic acid are similar during total knee arthroplasty. Moreover, it is recommended that occlusion of drainage tube can be conducted for 2 hours in intra-articular route of tranexamic acid.

title: Correlation of matrix metalloproteinase 2 and 9 with the early performance of knee osteoarthritis cartilage under MRI
abstract: BACKGROUND: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have been shown to break the balance between the production and degradation of extracellular matrix by degrading collagen, gelatin, elastin and other macromolecules, which is the leading cause of bone and cartilage damage in rheumatic arthritis. OBJECTIVE: To determine the expression levels of MMP-2 and MM-9 in the rabbit knee osteoarthritis cartilage, and to analyze whether they are related to the early MRI performance. METHODS: Fifty healthy Japanese white rabbits free from osteoarthritis were enrolled and randomly divided into control group (n=10) and model group (n=40). The anterior and posterior cruciate ligament amputation was adopted to establish the model of osteoarthritis. Subsequently, MRI examination and the expression levels of MMP-2 and MMP-9 were detected at 1, 3, 5 and 7 weeks (n=10 at each time point), respectively. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION: MRI examination showed that more damaged cartilage appeared with time in the rabbit model of osteoarthritis, and significantly different from MRI classification (P < 0.05). The expression levels of MMP-2 and MMP-9 mRNA in the model group were always significantly higher than those in the control group (P < 0.05); MMP-2 level reached the highest at 3 weeks after modeling (P < 0.01), and then presented a slight decline; MMP-9 level peaked at 5 weeks after modeling (P < 0.01) and slightly decreased at 7 weeks. MRI classification of cartage injury and expressions of MMP-2 (R2=0.119, P=0.119) and MMP-9 (R2= 0.466, P=0.466) were shown to have the correlation. These results illustrate that the serum levels of MMP-2 and MMP-9 are related to the early destruction of articular cartilage in patients with osteoarthritis, and can be used as predictors for early osteoarthritis.

title: Biological properties of bone morphogenetic proteins and basic fibroblast growth factor in biological materials for repair of articular cartilage defect
abstract: BACKGROUND: Articular cartilage regeneration can be regulated by autocrine or paracrine secretion of various cytokines. OBJECTIVE: To analyze biological properties of bone morphogenetic proteins and basic fibroblast growth factor in biological materials for repair of articular cartilage defect. METHODS: Forty New Zealand white rabbits were used and equally randomized into four groups: fibrin, basic fibroblast growth factor, bone morphogenetic protein, and combined treatment (basic fibroblast growth factor combined with bone morphogenetic protein) groups, respectively. Bioactive scaffolds with fibrin, basic fibroblast growth factor, bone morphogenetic protein, and basic fibroblast growth factor combined with bone morphogenetic protein were injected to repair the articular cartilage defect. Therapeutic effect and biological properties of biological materials were compared. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION: (1) In the fibrin group, two rabbits appeared to have limps. In the basic fibroblast growth factor group hand function was limited in one rabbit. In the bone morphogenetic protein group, one had a limp and one was in a limitation of activity. In the combined treatment group, rabbits recovered well and showed no differences in the knee joint before and after surgery (P < 0.05). (2) General observation: In the combined treatment group, soft solution cartilage defects disappeared, and angiogenesis and cartilage were similar with normal tissues. In the bone morphogenetic protein group, fractured cartilage marginal existed and could not be closely integrated with normal cartilage. The presence of chondrocytes in the periphery of the defect was seen under light microscope. In the fibrin group, defect site and surrounding tissues healed. In the basic fibroblast growth factor group, defect was repaired, but not smooth. (3) Results of hematoxylin and eosin staining: In the fibrin group, the bone defect was not repaired, obvious depression surface was seen. In basic fibroblast growth factor group, repair of cartilage defect was obvious. There were a lot of chondrocytes. In the bone morphogenetic protein group, the bone defect was repaired; chondrocytes appeared, but irregular arrangement. In the combined treatment group, good bone defect repair and a large number of cartilage cells were seen. Taken together, biological materials with fibrin and basic fibroblast growth factor are ideal for repair of articular cartilage defect by promoting formation of cartilage by bone morphogenetic protein and enhancing chondrocyte proliferation by basic fibroblast growth factor.

title: Application and safety of tranexamic acid in total knee arthroplasty
abstract: BACKGROUND: Studies suggested that blood loss was great during total knee arthroplasty, even blood transfusion was needed. Application of the tourniquet will destroy the coagulation system, and is not conducive to hemostasis after replacement. Recently, tranexamic acid has been extensively used to reduce blood loss during total knee arthroplasty, because of low price, simple administration pathway, and effective effects on hemostasis. OBJECTIVE: To summarize the application and safety of tranexamic acid in total knee arthroplasty. METHODS: The first author retrieved PubMed and Chinese Journal Full Text Database for articles from inception to October 2015. The key words were tranexamic acid, total knee arthroplasty, hemorrhage. More than 200 articles were retrieved, and finally 50 articles met the inclusion criteria. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION: Tranexamic acid is a fibrinolytic inhibitor, can reversibly block the binding of plasminogen to fibrin, effectively inhibit fibrinolysis, and reduce hemorrhage after total knee arthroplasty. Nevertheless, there were significant differences in the use, dose and effect of tranexamic acid on hemostasis among different studies. Tranexamic acid was an effective drug for hemostasis during total knee arthroplasty. During total knee arthroplasty, tranexamic acid had been used to reduce dominant blood loss and hidden blood loss after arthroplasty, and could not increase the risk for venous thrombosis of lower limb. Currently, the timing of use, dosage, route of administration, and possible complications of tranexamic acid remain controversial.

title: Revision total knee arthroplasty
abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is one of the most frequently preformed orthopaedic operations in the world. As the demand for TKA continues to increase, so will the need for revision TKA. This review focuses on revision TKAs, highlighting recent, key articles exploring the epidemiology, complications, blood loss, methods of pain control and patient-perceived outcomes from revision TKA. Surgical techniques aimed at addressing specific challenges including bone loss, exposure and implant choices are also discussed.

title: Myocardial heterogeneity in heart with postinfarction LV remodeling and its response to cell therapy
abstract: Rationale and Objective: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) hold promise for myocardial repair following injury. Here, we investigated the functional impact and myocardial heterogeneity of bioenergetics using a porcine model of post infarction LV remodeling, and 2 dimensional chemical shift imaging (2D CSI) P-31 MR spectroscopy. Methods and Results: Ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury was surgically induced by occlusion distal LAD (OCCL) for 60 minutes in female Yorkshire farm swine (≈15kg), then randomly assigned to experimental groups: 1) 16 million human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC) derived cardio myocytes (CMs), smooth muscle cells (SMC) and Endothelia cells (ECs) were directly myocardial injected through an epicardial fibrin patch (P+Cell, n= 4), 2) open patch (fibrin patch with no cell) were placed over the injury site (P w/o Cell, n=4). Size matched normal (n=9) and OCCL only (n=5) pigs were also studied. Four weeks after I/R, 2D CSI MRS studies were performed in a 9.4T/ 65 cm bore magnet. In vivo myocardial energetic mapping was achieved using 31P 2D CSI. To measure the forward flux rate PCr to ATP, 2D CSI data were acquired with or without saturation on ATPγ resonance. I/R injury has a heterogeneous effect on LV myocardial bioenergetics. Myocardial creatine phosphate (PCr)/ATP ratio is significantly decreased in border zone (BZ) of the infarction than the myocardial areas remote from the scar (RZ) in cell treated and patch only groups (1.54+/- 0.05 vs 2.25 +/- 0.10, 1.49+/-0.07 vs 2.34 +/- 0.07, BZ vs RZ, p<0.05). The BZ PCr/ATP ratio is improved in the cell treated group compared with open patch group (1.71 +/- 0.05 vs. 1.54 +/- 0.05, p<0.05). The forward flux rate constant of PCr/ATP (kpcr→ATP ) in the border zone is slightly increased in cell treated group compared with patch only group (0.29 +/- 0.02 vs 0.22 +/- 0.04 , p<0.05) Conclusion: The approach of 2D CSI 31P MRS can effectively map the heterogeneity of myocardial ATP flux rate via CK In Vivo porcine hearts. Postinfarction LV remodeling heart manifests pronounced heterogeneity in myocardial bioenergetics with most severe alterations in BZ. Cell therapy may effectively improve BZ myocardial bioenergetics.

title: Dosing of rivaroxaban by indication: Getting the right dose for the patient
abstract: Introduction: Vitamin K antagonists were the only oral anticoagulants available for several decades, but they require frequent coagulation monitoring and dose adjustment. The direct oral anticoagulants rivaroxaban, dabigatran, apixaban, and, most recently, edoxaban have been approved for the management of specific thromboembolic indications.Areas covered: This review will provide a brief overview of the cell-based coagulation model, the main determinants of arterial and venous thrombosis, and the pharmacological rationale and clinical evidence for the different dosing regimens of rivaroxaban. Published articles indexed on PubMed and Medline covering arterial and venous thrombi pathophysiology, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of rivaroxaban, and Phase II and Phase III clinical studies with rivaroxaban as well as real-world evidence were analyzed.Expert opinion: Education on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic characteristics, as well as how to manage adverse events, is needed to increase physician knowledge and confidence in using direct oral anticoagulants, as specifically discussed for rivaroxaban in this article. The continued uptake of direct oral anticoagulants in clinical practice depends on understanding of the clinical evidence and reassurance provided by emerging real-world data.

title: Bone-specific gene expression patterns and whole bone tissue of female mice are programmed by early life exposure to soy isoflavones and folic acid
abstract: Female mice exposed to soy isoflavones (ISO) during early postnatal life have improved bone outcomes at adulthood. Since long-lasting effects may be mediated by DNA methylation, we hypothesized that providing supplemental folic acid (FA), a methyl donor, during early life, would enhance the positive effect of ISO to bone health. Bone-specific gene expression patterns were studied to understand potential mechanisms. CD-1 dams (. n=36) were randomized to adequate or supplemental levels of FA (2 or 8 mg/kg diet) during pregnancy and lactation, and offspring received corn oil or ISO (7 mg/kg body weight/d) from postnatal day 1 to 10. From weaning, pups were fed an adequate FA diet and were studied to 4 months of age. Female offspring exposed to supplemental FA+ISO had higher bone mineral density (BMD), trabecular connectivity and peak load at the lumbar spine compared to females exposed to adequate FA. Female offspring exposed to adequate FA+ISO or supplemental FA had higher (. P<.05) BMD and greater resistance to fracture at the lumbar spine and the femur; higher trabecular connectivity at the lumbar spine and lower expression of DNA methyltransferase 3a (Dnmt3a) and neuropeptide Y (NPY) in the femur compared to mice exposed to adequate FA. In addition, only mice exposed to adequate FA+ISO had microstructural improvements at the femur neck and higher serum osteoprotegrin (OPG) and insulin growth factor-I (IGF-I). In summary, exposure to supplemental FA did not enhance the positive effect of ISO in bone. However, exposure to adequate FA+ISO or supplemental FA improved bone at least in part by suppressing Dnmt3a and NPY.

title: The role of electronic healthcare record databases in paediatric drug safety surveillance: A retrospective cohort study
abstract: Aim Electronic healthcare record (EHR)-based surveillance systems are increasingly being developed to support early detection of safety signals. It is unknown what the power of such a system is for surveillance among children and adolescents. In this paper we provide estimates of the number and classes of drugs, and incidence rates (IRs) of events, that can be monitored in children and adolescents (0-18 years). Methods Data were obtained from seven population-based EHR databases in Denmark, Italy, and the Netherlands during the period 1996-2010. We estimated the number of drugs for which specific adverse events can be monitored as a function of actual drug use, minimally detectable relative risk (RR) and IRs for 10 events. Results The population comprised 4 838 146 individuals (25 575 132 person years (PYs)), who were prescribed 2170 drugs (1 610 631 PYs drug-exposure). Half of the total drug-exposure in PYs was covered by only 18 drugs (0.8%). For a relatively frequent event like upper gastrointestinal bleeding there were 39 drugs for which an association with a RR ≥4, if present, could be investigated. The corresponding number of drugs was eight for a rare event like anaphylactic shock. Conclusion Drug use in children is rare and shows little variation. The number of drugs with enough exposure to detect rare adverse events in children and adolescents within an EHR-based surveillance system such as EU-ADR is limited. Use of additional sources of paediatric drug exposure information and global collaboration are imperative in order to optimize EHR data for paediatric safety surveillance.

title: Haemostatic function and biomarkers of endothelial damage before and after RBC transfusion in patients with haematologic disease
abstract: Background and objectives: Transfusion of red blood cells (RBC) is beneficial for the patient but can also be harmful, as randomized trials have demonstrated increased infection rates, bleeding and mortality. The study aim was to investigate the response of the vascular system (the haemostatic function and the endothelium) to RBC transfusion. Materials and Methods: Blood was sampled from patients with various transfusion-dependent haematologic diseases before 1 and 24 h after RBC transfusion. Primary and secondary haemostasis was evaluated by whole-blood impedance aggregometry (Multiplate) and by thromboelastography (TEG). Samples were analysed by ELISA for biomarkers reflecting endothelial activation and damage (sICAM-1, syndecan-1, sThrombomodulin (sTM), sVE-Cadherin), platelet activation (sCD40L) and inflammation (hsCRP). Results: A total of 58 patients were enrolled in the study. Median age was 71 years. Compared to before transfusion, patients had slightly reduced coagulability 1 h after RBC transfusion, assessed by TEG.
